summary: A topological sort lists the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that every edge points forward: for each edge u to v, u appears before v. It exists exactly when the graph has no directed cycle, which makes the algorithm double as a cycle detector. You meet it in build systems, course prerequisites, spreadsheet recalculation, package managers, and as the first step of dynamic programming over a DAG.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
Many tasks have dependencies: you must put on socks before shoes, compile a library before the program that links it, take Algorithms before Advanced Algorithms. Model each task as a vertex and each 'must come before' as a directed edge. A **topological order** is any sequence that respects every edge.

Two facts frame everything else. First, an order exists if and only if the graph is a DAG. A cycle such as A before B before C before A is impossible to satisfy. Second, the order is usually not unique. Whenever two vertices have no path between them, either can come first. A path graph has exactly one order, while a graph with no edges has V factorial of them.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **DAG**: a directed graph with no directed cycle. Topological sorting is defined only for DAGs.
**In-degree**: the number of edges entering a vertex. A vertex with in-degree 0 has no unmet prerequisite.
**Source and sink**: a source has in-degree 0; a sink has out-degree 0. Every non-empty DAG has at least one of each.
**Kahn's algorithm**: repeatedly remove a vertex with in-degree 0 and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees (BFS style).
**DFS-based sort**: run depth-first search and list vertices by decreasing finish time (reverse post-order).
**Back edge**: an edge to a vertex that is still on the DFS recursion stack. It proves a cycle.
**Level (layer)**: vertices removed in the same Kahn round; they have no dependencies among themselves and can run in parallel.
**Linear extension**: the order-theory name for a topological order of a partial order.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body:
**Kahn's algorithm** keeps a queue of ready vertices. Compute all in-degrees, enqueue the zero ones, then repeat: pop u, output it, and for each edge u to v decrement v's in-degree; when v reaches 0 it becomes ready. If the output has fewer than V vertices at the end, the leftover vertices lie on or behind a cycle.

Example: edges 5 to 2, 5 to 0, 4 to 0, 4 to 1, 2 to 3, 3 to 1 on vertices 0..5. In-degrees: 0:2, 1:2, 2:1, 3:1, 4:0, 5:0. Queue starts [4, 5]. Pop 4: output 4; 0 drops to 1, 1 drops to 1. Pop 5: output 5; 2 drops to 0 (enqueue), 0 drops to 0 (enqueue). Pop 2: output 2; 3 drops to 0 (enqueue). Pop 0: output 0. Pop 3: output 3; 1 drops to 0 (enqueue). Pop 1: output 1. Order: 4, 5, 2, 0, 3, 1. All six vertices came out, so there is no cycle.

**DFS-based sort** uses three colors. Start a DFS from each unvisited vertex. A vertex is gray while its recursion is active and black when done. Meeting a gray vertex means a back edge and therefore a cycle. When a vertex finishes, every vertex reachable from it has already finished, so putting it in front of the finished ones keeps all edges pointing forward.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Kahn (BFS)**: iterative, detects cycles by counting, and exposes the layers. Prefer it when recursion depth could overflow or when you want parallel batches.
**DFS reverse post-order**: short to code recursively and integrates well with other DFS work such as strongly connected components.
**Lexicographically smallest order**: replace Kahn's queue with a min-heap so the smallest ready vertex is always chosen. Costs O((V + E) log V).
**All topological orders**: backtrack over the ready set, choosing each ready vertex in turn. The count can be factorial, so this is only for small graphs.
**Layered (level) order**: process Kahn one whole level at a time; the number of levels is the length of the longest path plus one.
**Online / incremental**: maintaining an order while edges are inserted is a separate problem (Pearce-Kelly, Marchetti-Spaccamela algorithms).
**Partial order with cycles**: condense strongly connected components first (Tarjan or Kosaraju); the component graph is a DAG you can sort.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: Time: O(V + E) for both Kahn and DFS; every vertex and edge is touched a constant number of times.
Space: O(V) for in-degrees, queue or state array, and the output, plus O(V + E) for the adjacency lists.
Heap-based smallest order: O((V + E) log V).
Number of orders: between 1 and V factorial. A graph with V vertices in a single chain has 1; the empty graph has V factorial. Counting all orders in general is #P-complete.
Recursion depth of the DFS version reaches V on a chain, so at V = 1,000,000 an explicit stack is safer in C.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Ignoring the cycle check**: Kahn silently returns a short list on cyclic input. Always compare the output length with V.
**Wrong edge direction**: for 'course b requires a', add edge a to b, not b to a. Reversing it gives the reversed order, a classic off-by-meaning bug.
**Marking only visited / not visited in DFS**: undirected-style two-state tracking misses cycles or falsely reports them on cross edges. Directed graphs need the 'on stack' state.
**Assuming uniqueness**: tests that compare against one specific order fail. Verify the property (every edge goes forward) instead.
**Disconnected graphs**: start DFS from every unvisited vertex; Kahn handles this automatically.
**Duplicate edges**: they inflate in-degree consistently, so Kahn still works; just do not de-duplicate on one side only.
**Stack overflow**: recursive DFS on a million-node chain overflows the default stack.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Build systems**: make, Bazel, Ninja and Gradle order compilation units and run independent ones in parallel by layer.
**Package managers**: apt, npm, cargo and pip resolve install order from dependency edges and report cycles.
**Spreadsheets**: a cell's formula depends on other cells; recalculation follows a topological order, and a cycle becomes a circular-reference error.
**Task schedulers and data pipelines**: Airflow DAGs, CI pipelines and database query plans order stages this way.
**Compilers**: instruction scheduling, symbol resolution and dead-code analysis operate on dependency DAGs.
**Databases and migrations**: foreign-key dependencies decide the order to create, load or drop tables.
**Makefiles**: each prerequisite has an edge to its target; make rebuilds a target only after its prerequisites, and `-j` runs independent targets in parallel.

**Operating systems**: draw an edge from process A to process B when A waits for a resource B holds; a deadlock is exactly a cycle in this wait-for graph, so a failed topological sort reports it. The same check finds circular imports and circular foreign keys.
**Precedence-constrained optimization**: any problem phrased as 'do A before B' for many pairs, such as university course planning, is a direct application.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Can every directed graph be topologically sorted?** No, only DAGs.
**How do you detect a cycle?** Kahn outputs fewer than V vertices, or DFS finds an edge to a gray vertex.
**Is the order unique?** Only if consecutive vertices in it are joined by an edge, that is, the order forms a Hamiltonian path.
**Time complexity?** O(V + E).
**Why does reverse finish time work?** If there is an edge u to v, then v finishes before u in a DFS, so reversing puts u first.
**Longest path in a DAG?** Process in topological order and relax, O(V + E). It is NP-hard on general graphs.

subtopics.title: Kahn's algorithm in depth
subtopics.summary: Peel off zero in-degree vertices one layer at a time.

sections.body:
Think of deleting a vertex and its outgoing edges. The graph left over is still a DAG, so it still has a source. Kahn simulates that deletion with an in-degree counter instead of modifying the graph: decrementing the count is the same as erasing the edge. The queue holds exactly the vertices whose prerequisites are all done. Because each edge is decremented once and each vertex is enqueued once, the work is O(V + E).

A stack instead of a queue still yields a valid order, only a different one. Pick the container by the property you want: queue for level-by-level, min-heap for smallest-first, stack for depth-first flavor.

subtopics.title: DFS-based topological sort
subtopics.summary: Reverse post-order of a depth-first search.

sections.body:
Run DFS and record each vertex at the moment it finishes. The finishing times satisfy a key property: for any edge u to v in a DAG, finish(v) < finish(u). Sorting by decreasing finish time therefore puts every u before its successor v.

The code writes into the output array from the back, which avoids a final reverse. The three-state coloring is essential: state 1 means 'on the current path', and reaching it again means a cycle. A finished vertex (state 2) reached through a different route is a harmless forward or cross edge.

subtopics.title: Cycle detection
subtopics.summary: The same algorithms prove whether the graph is a DAG.

sections.body:
In Kahn, a cycle keeps every vertex on it from ever reaching in-degree 0, so the output stops short. The vertices that never leave contain all cycle vertices and everything reachable only through them.

In DFS, a back edge to a gray vertex is a cycle. To report the cycle itself, keep a parent array and walk back from the current vertex to the gray target. For undirected graphs this does not apply: use union-find or DFS with parent tracking instead, since an undirected edge is trivially a two-vertex cycle in the directed view.

subtopics.title: Course schedule problems
subtopics.summary: The classic interview form of the algorithm.

sections.body: **Course Schedule**: given prerequisite pairs, return true if all courses can be finished. That is only a cycle check: run Kahn and compare the count with the number of courses. **Course Schedule II** returns one valid order, which is Kahn's output. **Minimum semesters** is the number of Kahn levels, and **parallel courses with a limit per semester** needs a priority on longest remaining chain. Always build the graph with edge prerequisite to course, and keep an array of in-degrees sized to the number of courses.

subtopics.title: Alien dictionary and string orderings
subtopics.summary: Derive the graph from the data, then sort it.

sections.body: Given words sorted in an unknown alphabet, compare each adjacent pair; the first position where they differ gives one edge 'letter in the first word comes before letter in the second'. Run Kahn over the set of letters that appear. Two traps: if a longer word precedes its own prefix (for example 'abc' before 'ab'), the input is invalid, and a cycle among letters also means no valid alphabet. The result is any valid order, so the problem usually asks you to accept multiple answers.

subtopics.title: Longest path and DP over a DAG
subtopics.summary: Topological order turns dependency graphs into simple dynamic programs.

sections.body: When subproblems form a DAG, evaluating them in topological order guarantees that every dependency is ready. The same pattern gives shortest paths with negative weights on a DAG, the critical path in project scheduling (CPM), and counting paths between two vertices.

The critical path of a project is the longest weighted path through the task DAG. Its length is the minimum possible completion time with unlimited workers. Tasks on it have zero slack, so delaying one delays the project.

subtopics.title: Parallel scheduling by levels
subtopics.summary: Kahn rounds expose what can run at the same time.

sections.body: Process the queue in whole rounds: take every vertex currently ready, finish them together, then decrement their neighbours. Each round is a batch with no internal dependencies, so a build tool can launch it in parallel. The number of rounds equals the longest path measured in vertices, which is the best possible depth with unlimited workers. With a limited worker count, the schedule becomes NP-hard in general, and real tools use heuristics such as always starting the task with the longest remaining chain.

subtopics.title: Lexicographically smallest and all orders
subtopics.summary: Control which valid order you get.

sections.body: Use a min-heap in Kahn to take the smallest ready vertex each time. This yields the lexicographically smallest order and is the usual answer for problems such as 'smallest valid task order'. To enumerate every order, recurse: for each currently ready vertex, remove it, recurse, then restore its neighbours' in-degrees. The running time is proportional to the number of orders, which may be factorial. To get the largest order instead, flip the heap to a max-heap.

subtopics.title: Why only DAGs have a topological order
subtopics.summary: Undirected edges and cycles both make an order impossible.

sections.body: For an undirected edge u-v you can read it as u to v and as v to u, so nothing says which endpoint must come first: the idea of a dependency disappears. For a directed cycle u to v to w to u, you would need u before v, v before w and w before u, which no linear arrangement can satisfy. Anything that is both directed and acyclic works. The order represents dependencies, which is different from the visit order of a plain DFS or BFS: a BFS from one vertex may list a vertex before something it depends on.

subtopics.title: Worked example from an adjacency list
subtopics.summary: Reading the graph from an array of neighbour lists.

sections.body:
Let adj = [[1], [2], [], [2, 4], []]. Row i lists the targets of vertex i, so the edges are 0 to 1, 1 to 2, 3 to 2 and 3 to 4. In-degrees: 0:0, 1:1, 2:2, 3:0, 4:1. Vertices 0 and 3 have no incoming edges, so both can start.

Kahn's run: queue [0, 3]. Pop 0, output it; vertex 1 drops to 0 and is queued. Pop 3, output it; vertex 2 drops from 2 to 1 and vertex 4 drops to 0 and is queued. Pop 1, output it; vertex 2 drops to 0 and is queued. Pop 4. Pop 2. The order is [0, 3, 1, 4, 2]. Vertex 1 depends only on 0, vertex 4 only on 3, and vertex 2 on both 1 and 3, so it must come last. Other valid orders exist, such as [3, 0, 4, 1, 2], because vertices with no path between them may swap. In a small graph where 4 and 5 both feed 3, which feeds 1, both 4, 5, 3, 1 and 5, 4, 3, 1 are valid, so check the forward-edge property rather than comparing with one fixed answer.

subtopics.title: DFS with a stack: push after the children
subtopics.summary: The stack-based formulation of the DFS method.

sections.body: Run DFS and push a vertex onto a stack only after all its neighbours have been visited and pushed. When the search is over, popping the stack yields the order, because a vertex always sits above everything that depends on it. On adj = [[1], [2], [], [2, 4], []], a DFS from 0 visits 1 then 2, pushing 2, 1, 0 in finish order; DFS from 3 finds 2 already done, visits 4, then pushes 4 and 3. The stack from bottom to top is 2, 1, 0, 4, 3, so popping gives 3, 4, 0, 1, 2, which is also valid. Remember to start a search from every unvisited vertex, because the graph may be disconnected.

subtopics.title: Validating a computed order
subtopics.summary: A short checker to test any implementation.

sections.body: Because many orders are valid, test by property. Record each vertex's position in the output, then confirm that every edge goes to a later position and that the output contains each vertex exactly once.

takeaways: A topological order exists if and only if the directed graph has no cycle.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove in-degree 0 vertices; fewer than V outputs means a cycle.
DFS version: list vertices by decreasing finish time; an edge to a gray vertex is a cycle.
Both approaches run in O(V + E) time and O(V) extra space.
The order is generally not unique; use a min-heap in Kahn for the lexicographically smallest one.
For 'a is a prerequisite of b', draw the edge a to b; reversing it is the commonest bug.
Process vertices in topological order to do shortest or longest path DP on a DAG in O(V + E).
